saturation-excess overland flow.text: Runoff produced at once when rain keeps falling on soil that is already saturated and whose surface hollows are full.

subsurface return flow.text: Water that soaks into a hillside upslope, flows sideways through the soil and seeps back out near a channel; also called throughflow.

urban runoff.text: Surface runoff from rain, landscape irrigation and car washing created by urbanization.

seasonal subsidence and heave.text: The sinking of the ground as clay-rich soils dry and shrink with the seasons, and its rise again when they rewet.

stormwater management.text: The control of both the quantity and the quality of stormwater.

stormwater sinkholes.text: Sinkhole collapses caused when urban stormwater drains down through karst ground and carries soil and rock fragments away.

rainfall-runoff model.text: A model of how rainfall on a drainage basin is converted into runoff.

hydrological transport model.text: A mathematical model that simulates the flow of rivers, streams, groundwater or drainage fronts and calculates water quality.

electrical double layer.text: The cloud of balancing cations that surrounds every negatively charged clay platelet, whose thickness depends on the salinity of the water.

hydrologic soil group.text: One of four classes, A to D, into which the NRCS sorts soils by how readily they take in water, used to choose a runoff curve number.

soil erosion.text: The wearing away of the upper layer of soil, a form of soil degradation.

runoff curve number.text: An empirical number, CN, used in hydrology to predict direct runoff or infiltration from rainfall excess.

water erosion.text: The removal of soil by rainfall and by the surface runoff it produces.

soil and water assessment tool.text: A free, open-source hydrology model and GIS simulation sponsored by the USDA, known as SWAT.

rainfall erosivity.text: The power of rainfall to cause soil erosion, set mainly by how much rain falls and how intensely.

wind erosion.text: Erosion by wind, which lifts and carries away loose particles (deflation) and wears down surfaces with windborne grains (abrasion).

erosion control.text: The practice of preventing or controlling wind and water erosion in farming, land development, coastal areas, river banks and construction.

dust.text: Fine particles of solid matter; on Earth, mostly particles in the air from soil lifted by wind, volcanic eruptions and pollution.

vegetation cover and erosion.text: The protection that living plants and the litter they leave give the soil against wind and water erosion.

agriculture and soil erosion.text: The acceleration of soil erosion by farming practices that loosen, bare or compact the soil.

erodibility.text: The inherent lack of resistance of a soil or rock to erosion.

climate change and soil erosion.text: The expected rise in soil erosion as warming brings heavier rainfall and alters vegetation, litter, soil moisture and frozen ground.

deforestation and soil erosion.text: The rise in soil erosion that follows removal of forest cover and its protective forest floor.

slope and erosion.text: The influence of a slope's steepness and length on how fast runoff flows and how much soil it erodes.

rill erosion.text: Erosion in rills, shallow channels no more than a few centimetres deep cut into soil by flowing surface water.

gully erosion.text: Erosion that cuts gullies, steep-sided channels formed in soil by running water, mass movement or both, usually on hillsides or in floodplains.

universal soil loss equation.text: A widely used empirical model (USLE) that estimates long-term average annual soil loss from water erosion as the product of six factors.

splash erosion.text: Erosion caused when falling raindrops strike bare soil and knock particles loose.

urbanization and erosion.text: The increase in erosion and polluted runoff caused by construction, roads and paved urban land.

erosion prediction.text: Using data and models to predict where, and how fast, erosion may happen in the future.

soil loss tolerance.text: The maximum average yearly soil loss, in tons per acre per year, that still lets a soil sustain current production economically and indefinitely; also called the T value.

mineral dust.text: An atmospheric aerosol of suspended soil minerals, mainly oxides and carbonates.

riparian buffer.text: A vegetated strip beside a stream, usually forested, that shades it and partly shields it from the effects of neighbouring land use.

geotextile.text: A permeable fabric laid with soil to separate, filter, reinforce, protect or drain it.

tillage erosion.text: Soil erosion in cultivated fields caused by the movement of soil during tillage.

jet erosion test.text: A geotechnical test, done in the field or the laboratory, that measures a soil's resistance to erosion with a jet of water.

dust control.text: The suppression of airborne solid particles smaller than 500 micrometres.

grassed waterway.text: A strip of native grassland 2 to 48 meters (6.6 to 157.5 feet) wide, laid along the lowest line of a cultivated dry valley to control erosion.

revegetation.text: The replanting and rebuilding of the soil of disturbed land.

prairie restoration.text: The work of restoring prairie destroyed by industrial, agricultural, commercial or residential development to its earlier state.

wepp.text: The Water Erosion Prediction Project model, a physically based erosion simulation built on hydrology, plant science, hydraulics and erosion mechanics.

rill initiation.text: The start of a rill, when the shear stress of runoff exceeds the soil's shear strength and water begins to tear particles loose.

sheet erosion.text: The even erosion of soil or other material across a wide area by a thin, unchannelled layer of flowing water.

support practice factor.text: The P factor of the Universal Soil Loss Equation, a soil loss ratio expressing how much conservation practices reduce erosion.

rainfall simulator.text: A device used in soil science and hydrology to study how soil reacts to rainfall.

post-fire hillslope stabilization.text: Treatments that steady burned slopes by offsetting fire's damage to vegetation and soil, to cut the risk of damaging runoff and erosion downhill.

tillage erosion measurement.text: Ways of quantifying tillage erosion, either by tracking soil moved by tillage or by measuring where soil is lost and gained.

tillage erosion models.text: Computer models that simulate how tillage moves soil along a hillslope or across a field.

sediment.text: Solid material made of loose particles that is carried to a new place and deposited there.

erosion.text: The removal of soil, rock or dissolved material from one place on the Earth's surface by processes such as flowing water or wind, and its transport to another place where it is deposited.

erosion index.text: Potential erosion from all sources except gullies divided by the soil's T value, the erosion rate above which long-term productivity may suffer; also called the erodibility index.

revised universal soil loss equation.text: A revised form of the Universal Soil Loss Equation, known as RUSLE, still used to estimate soil erosion.

wind erosion equation.text: A model that estimates a field's potential average annual soil loss to wind, used to design wind erosion control.

aeolian processes.text: The erosion, transport and deposition of sediment by wind at or near the Earth's surface.

sediment control.text: A practice or device that keeps eroded soil on a construction site so it does not wash off and pollute nearby waters.

sediment pollution of waterways.text: The harm done to rivers, lakes, coasts and their life by excess sediment washed in from eroding soil.

mass wasting.text: The movement of rock or soil down slopes under the force of gravity; also called mass movement.

downhill creep.text: The slow downward movement of soil and rock on a gentle slope; also called soil creep.

slope stability.text: The ability of a soil or rock slope to withstand movement; the opposite condition is slope instability or slope failure.

landslide.text: Any of several forms of mass wasting with relatively rapid ground movement, such as rockfalls, mudflows, slope failures and debris flows.

sediment transport.text: The movement of solid particles, from clay to boulders, by gravity together with the water, air or ice in which they are carried.

sediment grain shape.text: The description of sediment particles by three parameters: overall form (sphericity), roundness of corners and surface texture.

sediment delivery ratio.text: The fraction of gross erosion on a catchment (interrill, rill, gully and stream erosion) expected to reach the river outlet.

chemical erosion.text: The loss of material from a landscape in dissolved form, as solutes.

coastal erosion.text: The wearing away of shorelines, mainly by currents and waves, with changes in sea level also playing a part.

glacial erosion.text: Erosion by moving glacier ice, mainly through abrasion, plucking and ice thrusting.

landslide classification.text: A scheme sorting landslides into six types of movement (fall, topple, slide, spread, flow and slope deformation), each found in both rock and soil.

internal erosion.text: The formation of voids inside a soil as seeping water removes material.

river and stream erosion.text: Erosion by water flowing continuously along a linear channel, which deepens valleys and wears away river banks.

solifluction.text: Gradual downslope mass movement of soil linked to freezing and thawing.

quick clay.text: A highly sensitive glaciomarine clay, also called Leda or Champlain Sea clay, that can change from a solid into a watery fluid when disturbed.

debris flow.text: A water-laden mass of soil and broken rock that flows down mountainsides, funnels into channels and leaves thick muddy deposits on valley floors.

deposition (geology).text: The geological process by which sediment, soil and rock are added to a landform or landmass.

aeolian transport.text: The movement of sediment by wind through suspension, saltation (skipping) and creep (rolling or sliding).

deflation.text: The lifting and removal of loose surface material by turbulent wind.

sand dune.text: A mound or ridge of sediment heaped up by the wind, independent of any obstacle.

wind abrasion.text: The wearing of rock and landforms by wind-driven grains, also called corrasion.

climate change and landslides.text: The effects of changing temperature, rainfall and evapotranspiration on where, how often and how strongly landslides occur.

landslide hazard mapping.text: Analysing the factors behind past landslides to map where future ones are likely, to reduce losses and guide land-use planning.

dust bowl.text: A decade of severe dust storms and drought, 1930–1940, that badly damaged the farming and ecology of the High Plains and North American prairies.

dust storm.text: A storm in which strong wind blows loose sand and dirt off dry ground, common in arid and semi-arid regions; also called a sandstorm.

landslide monitoring.text: Tracking slope movement to judge danger, issue timely alerts and plan protective measures.

shallow and deep-seated landslides.text: Landslides grouped by the depth of their sliding surface: within the soil mantle or weathered bedrock (shallow), or well below tree rooting depth (deep-seated).

silt fence.text: A temporary fabric fence used on construction sites to keep sediment carried by stormwater runoff out of nearby waters.

denudation.text: The sum of processes by which moving water, ice, wind and waves wear down the Earth's surface, lowering its elevation and relief.

dust bowl government response.text: The US federal programmes of the 1930s that answered the Dust Bowl with soil conservation, tree planting and farm relief.

economic legacy of the dust bowl.term: Economic legacy of the Dust Bowl
economic legacy of the dust bowl.text: The lasting fall in farmland value and population that followed the Dust Bowl's loss of topsoil.

earthflow.text: A viscous downslope flow of water-saturated fine-grained material moving under gravity.

sedimentation.text: The settling of suspended particles out of a fluid until they come to rest against a barrier.

siltation.text: Water pollution by fine silt and clay particles, both as raised suspended sediment and as unwanted fine deposits on the bottom.

river bank failure.text: The sudden mass wasting of a stream bank, when gravity on its rock and soil exceeds the cohesive and adhesive forces holding them together.

sediment basin.text: A temporary pond on a construction site that captures soil washed off in rain storms and protects the water quality of nearby waters.

mudflow.text: A fast-moving flow of debris and soil that has been liquefied by added water; also called a mudslide.

fluvial sediment processes.text: The movement of sediment by rivers and streams, with the erosion, deposition and landforms it creates.

gelifluction.text: The downslope movement of waterlogged topsoil driven by seasonal freezing and thawing, closely related to solifluction.

fiber roll.text: A temporary tube of straw, coconut fibre or similar material laid on construction slopes to control erosion and trap sediment.

sediment treatment systems.text: Systems that clear sediment-laden construction runoff by adding flocculants and then filtering or settling the water.

marine clay.text: Marine clays are fine-grained sedimentary deposits made mostly of clay minerals that build up in coastal environments.

saltation.text: A mode of transport in which wind or water lifts loose grains from a bed and carries them in short hops back to the surface.

hole erosion test.text: A geotechnical laboratory test of a soil's resistance to erosion, used above all for internal erosion in embankment dams.

gully stabilisation.text: Altering water flow through a gully to reduce scouring, let sediment build up and allow plants to return.

vegetation and slope stability.text: The two-way link between slopes and the plants growing on them, which can either strengthen or weaken a slope.

slope stability analysis.text: Static or dynamic, analytical or empirical methods for evaluating the stability of natural slopes and of dams, embankments and excavations in soil and rock.

slope stabilization.text: Engineering work on slopes that raises their stability and lessens the effect of landslides.

mass wasting landforms.text: The deposits and landforms left by mass wasting, usually subtle but occasionally spectacular.

baer–babinet law.text: The idea that the Earth's rotation influences how rivers form, making them erode one bank more than the other.

soil sloughing.text: The falling of soil off banks and slopes when it loses cohesion.

fluvio-thermal erosion.text: The combined mechanical and thermal erosion of ice-rich soils and sediments by an unfrozen river or stream.

tdr in geotechnical monitoring.text: The use of time-domain reflectometry to watch for slope movement at highway cuts, rail beds and open-pit mines.

suspended load.text: The part of a flow's sediment that is lifted off the bed and held up in the fluid by turbulence.

stream power.text: The energy that flowing water in a river or stream expends on its bed and banks, first derived by R. A. Bagnold in the 1960s.

bed load and suspended load.text: The two main ways a flow carries sediment: rolling and sliding along the bed as bed load, or held up in the water as suspended load.

hjulström curve.text: A graph, drawn by Filip Hjulström in 1935, of the flow velocity needed to erode, transport or deposit sediment of each grain size.

fech fech.text: A very fine powder formed by the erosion of clay-limestone terrain, found mostly in deserts.

bank erosion.text: The wearing away of the banks of a stream or river, as distinct from scour of its bed.

desert pavement.text: A desert surface covered with closely packed, interlocking pebble- and cobble-sized rock fragments.

shear strength of discontinuities.text: The shear strength along a discontinuity, such as a joint, in a soil or rock mass, which strongly shapes how the mass behaves.

quick clay formation.text: The sequence by which glacial rock flour, laid down loosely in the sea and later raised above it, became a weak and water-rich clay.

quick clay landslides.text: Landslides in quick clay, which are retrogressive: they usually start at water and work their way upslope.

legacy sediment.text: Bodies of sediment laid down as a result of human activity since the Neolithic.

river bank protection.text: The structural and vegetative measures used to keep river banks from eroding and failing.

headward erosion.text: Erosion at the head of a stream channel that moves its origin upslope, lengthening the stream, valley or gully and enlarging its drainage basin.

aggradation.text: The rise in land elevation, usually in a river system, as sediment is deposited; also called alluviation.

entrainment.text: The incorporation of surface sediment into a moving fluid such as air, water or ice, as part of erosion.

shear velocity.text: A shear stress rewritten in units of velocity, also called friction velocity.

badlands.text: Dry terrain in which soft sedimentary rocks and clay-rich soils have been deeply eroded into steep, bare ground.

measuring denudation rates.text: The estimation of how fast a landscape is being lowered, usually expressed in centimetres or inches per 1000 years.

shields parameter.text: A dimensionless number used to calculate when sediment begins to move in a fluid flow.

corrasion.text: Mechanical erosion of the land surface by material dragged across it by running water, waves, glaciers, wind or downslope movement.

marine clay flocculation.text: Flocculation is the process by which fine particles in water clump together into flocs.

marine clay in construction.text: Building on marine clay is a geotechnical challenge because the soil is open, sensitive and weak under load.

root reinforcement of soil.text: The strengthening of soil by roots that grow across potential failure planes, act as piles and limit surface erosion.

root pull-out resistance.text: The force a root resists before being pulled out of the ground, usually only a little less than its laboratory tensile strength.

transpiration and slope stability.text: The stabilising of slopes by plants that draw water out of the soil and transpire it, lowering soil pore water pressure.

landslide causes and triggers.text: The distinction between the conditions that make a slope vulnerable to failure (causes) and the single event that finally sets it moving (trigger).

rainfall-triggered landslides.text: Landslides set off by heavy or prolonged rain, the main trigger in most cases.

sediment yield.text: The quantity of sediment per unit area of a watershed that a river removes over a period of time.

soil piping.text: The progressive internal erosion of soil by seeping water, which carves subsurface pipes that discharge water downstream.

vegetative filter strip.text: A strip of grass or other permanent vegetation that shields riparian areas from runoff carrying sediment, pesticides, pathogens and nutrients.

wetland.text: A semi-aquatic ecosystem whose ground is flooded or saturated, permanently or seasonally, so that oxygen-poor processes take place in its soils.

peatland.text: A wetland whose soils consist of organic matter from decaying plants, forming layers of peat.

hydric soil.text: Soil that is permanently or seasonally saturated with water, so that it turns anaerobic, as in wetlands.

landscape ecology.text: The science of how ecological processes relate to particular ecosystems across a range of landscape scales and spatial patterns.

marsh.text: A wetland dominated by herbaceous rather than woody plants.

swamp.text: A forested wetland, with saturated soils or standing water dominated by water-tolerant woody plants.

floodplain.text: Land beside a river, from the channel banks to the valley sides, that floods when discharge is high.

ombrotrophic.text: Describing soils or vegetation that receive all their water and nutrients from precipitation rather than from streams or springs.

salt marsh.text: A tidal wetland in the upper intertidal zone, regularly flooded by seawater or brackish water and dominated by salt-tolerant plants.

bog.text: A wetland that accumulates peat, a deposit of dead plant material, often sphagnum moss.

muskeg.text: A peat-forming ecosystem of northern, mostly Arctic and boreal, climates, roughly synonymous with bog or peatland.

slump (geology).text: A form of mass wasting in which a coherent mass of loosely consolidated material or rock moves a short distance down a slope.

polder.text: A low-lying tract of land enclosed by dikes that forms an artificial hydrological unit.

riparian zone.text: The strip of land where a river or stream meets the land around it.

minerotrophic.text: Describing environments that get their nutrients mainly from groundwater flowing through mineral-rich soil or rock, or from surface water flowing over land.

fen.text: A peat-accumulating wetland fed by mineral-rich ground or surface water.

geomorphology.text: The scientific study of the origin and evolution of landforms created by physical, chemical or biological processes at or near Earth's surface.

bog–rich-fen gradient.text: The arrangement of bogs and fens along a gradient from poor to rich, with bogs at the poor end, extremely rich fens at the rich end and poor fens between.

wetland nutrient cycling.text: The cycling of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and other elements in wetland soils, which sit at the interface of oxygenated and oxygen-free environments.

peatland carbon storage.text: The accumulation of carbon in peatland soils, which makes peatlands the largest natural carbon store on land.

raised bog.text: An acidic, mineral-poor bog fed only by precipitation, whose peat has risen into a dome above the groundwater.

freshwater marsh.text: A non-forested marsh with shallow fresh water that is continuously or frequently flooded.

alluvial fan.text: A cone-shaped spread of sediment that fans out from a concentrated source, such as a narrow canyon opening onto a plain.

paludification.text: The most common way boreal peatlands form, as peat builds up on previously drier, vegetated mineral soils and turns forest, grassland or bare land into peatland.

prairie pothole.text: A marsh in one of the many shallow depressions left by glaciers across northern North America.

vernal pool.text: A seasonal marsh in a shallow depression that holds shallow water in winter and spring and may be completely dry by summer and fall.

wet meadow.text: A freshwater marsh that is regularly flooded but often dry in summer.

slope aspect.text: The compass direction that a land surface faces, also called exposure.

palsa.text: A peat mound with a permanently frozen core of peat and mineral soil, typical of mires in the zone of discontinuous permafrost.

land loss.text: The conversion of coastal land to open water by natural processes and human activities.

ramsar convention.text: An international treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands, also called the Convention on Wetlands.

landscape patch and mosaic.text: A patch is a relatively uniform area that differs from its surroundings; the mosaic is the whole pattern of patches, corridors and matrix that makes up a landscape.

ecotone.text: A transitional zone between two communities, one kind of boundary between landscape patches.

spatial heterogeneity.text: The uneven distribution of objects across a landscape, a measure of how its parts differ from one another.

blanket bog.text: Peatland that forms where high rainfall and low evapotranspiration let peat cover broad stretches of rolling ground, not just wet hollows.

börde.text: A region of highly fertile, loess-covered lowland in North Germany, a 'fertile plain'.

peat swamp forest.text: A tropical moist forest whose waterlogged soil keeps dead leaves and wood from fully decaying, building a thick layer of acidic peat.

constructed wetland.text: An artificial wetland built to treat sewage, greywater, stormwater runoff or industrial wastewater.

wetland ecosystem services.text: The benefits wetlands give society, such as carbon storage, water purification, flood control and wildlife habitat.

wetland greenhouse gas emissions.text: The release of methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide from wetland soils, which makes wetlands the largest natural source of atmospheric methane.

wetland hydrology.text: The flow, storage and chemistry of surface and ground water in a wetland, the main factor that produces wetlands.

wetland loss.text: The draining, filling and conversion of wetlands for agriculture, building and other uses.

mire.text: A peatland that is still actively forming peat.

shrub swamp.text: A freshwater wetland dominated by shrubs, too wet to become swamp forest but too dry or shallow to become marsh.

gilgai.text: A microrelief of mounds and depressions formed in expanding clay soils, whose depressions hold small seasonal pools.

hillslope evolution.text: The change over time in the erosion rates, erosion styles and shape of the slopes of hills and mountains.

flark.text: A depression or hollow within a bog, typically one of a series of parallel hollows separated by ridges called strings.

palustrine wetland.text: Any inland, non-tidal wetland whose ocean-derived salts stay below 0.5 parts per thousand.

floodplain soils.text: The soils of floodplains, which vary with small changes in elevation and swing between aerated and flooded states.

us legal hydric soil definition.text: In US federal law, a soil that, undrained, is saturated, flooded or ponded long enough in the growing season to become anaerobic and support water-loving vegetation.

suffosion.text: The washing of loose soil or sediment down through fissures in the rock beneath, one of the two processes that form subsidence sinkholes.

string bog.text: A bog of slightly raised ridges and islands carrying woody plants, alternating with flat, wet sedge mats.

hummock.text: A small knoll or mound above the surrounding ground, usually under 15 metres high and found in groups or fields.

soil-surface roughness.text: The vertical variations in the micro- and macro-relief of a soil surface, together with their statistical distribution.

hydrosere.text: The plant succession by which an area of open fresh water fills in and becomes land, ultimately woodland.

pedotope.text: The total soil component of the non-living matrix of an ecotope.

mima mounds.text: Low, flattened, circular to oval natural mounds of loose, unstratified, often gravelly sediment forming an overthickened A horizon.

hillslope sediment flux models.text: Numerical models of hillslope erosion that describe the sediment flux on a slope at a given time rather than how its form changes.

soil-mantled parabolic hills.text: Convex, soil-covered hills long held to reflect a steady-state balance between soil production and soil erosion.

irrigation.text: Applying controlled amounts of water to land to help grow crops, landscape plants and lawns.

crop rotation.text: Growing a series of different crops on the same land over successive growing seasons.

leaching (agriculture).text: The loss of water-soluble plant nutrients from soil, carried away by rain and irrigation water.

land reclamation.text: Creating new land from oceans, seas, riverbeds or lake beds; the result is called reclaimed land or land fill.

herbicide.text: A substance, commonly called a weed killer, used to control unwanted plants.

agricultural soil science.text: The branch of soil science that studies soil conditions as they bear on growing food and fibre.

potting soil.text: A substrate, also called growing medium or potting mix, used to grow plants in containers.

organic farming.text: A farming system that relies on natural, non-synthetic inputs such as compost, manure and green manure, with techniques such as crop rotation and mixed cropping.

surface irrigation.text: Irrigation in which water is spread over the soil surface by gravity.

monocropping.text: Growing a single crop year after year on the same land, also called continuous cropping.

fallow.text: Leaving arable land unsown for one or more growing cycles.

irrigation efficiency.text: The share of water applied to a field that the crop actually uses: field water efficiency is the water transpired by the crop divided by the water applied, times 100.

sprinkler irrigation.text: Irrigation in which water is piped to points in the field and sprayed overhead by high-pressure sprinklers or guns.

subirrigation.text: Irrigation by artificially raising the water table so that the soil is moistened from below the plants' root zone.

wastewater irrigation.text: Watering crops with recycled or untreated municipal wastewater, whose nutrients can also fertilize them.

regenerative agriculture.text: A conservation and rehabilitation approach to farming that aims to regenerate topsoil, raise biodiversity and strengthen the health of farm soil.

crop choice in rotations.text: Choosing the crops of a rotation by what each adds to or takes from the field: organic matter, nutrients, pest control and protection from erosion.

crop rotation and erosion control.text: The use of crop sequences, residue and fallow management within a rotation to cut soil lost to erosion, often alongside zero or reduced tillage.

mixed farming.text: Farming that combines growing crops with keeping livestock, which helps manage rotations and cycle nutrients.

polyculture.text: Growing two or more crops in the same place at the same time.

intercropping.text: Growing two or more crops at the same time in the same field, a form of polyculture.

sustainable agriculture.text: Farming that reduces environmental harm, sustains and expands natural resources and uses non-renewable resources productively.

nitrate leaching.text: The loss of nitrate from soil as drainage water carries the excess ions, which soils do not hold, down to groundwater, streams and the sea.

drip irrigation.text: A micro-irrigation method that lets water drip slowly to plant roots, from above or below the soil surface, placing it in the root zone to minimize evaporation.

soil solarization.text: A non-chemical pest control method that traps the sun's heat in soil until many soil-borne plant pathogens are killed or badly weakened.

precision agriculture.text: A farm management strategy that gathers and analyses data on time, place and individual plants or animals to fit decisions to variation across fields, for better efficiency, yield and sustainability.

integrated pest management.text: Pest control that combines non-chemical and chemical methods to keep pests in economic check while relying less on chemicals.

crop yield.text: The amount of a crop, or of a product such as milk or wool, produced per unit area of land.

green revolution.text: A period in which technology transfer initiatives produced a large increase in crop yields.

soil steam sterilization.text: A farming technique that fully or partly sterilizes soil with steam, in open fields or greenhouses.

shifting cultivation.text: A farming system in which a plot is cropped for a while and then abandoned to fallow regrowth while the cultivator moves to another plot.

rotation effect.text: Agronomists' name for the yield benefit that crops gain from being grown in rotation.

agricultural land reclamation.text: Reclaiming land from the sea or from wetlands to make farmland, the main driver of reclamation before industrialisation.

slash-and-burn agriculture.text: A form of shifting cultivation in which forest or woodland plants are cut and burned to create a field called a swidden.

herbicide persistence.text: How long a herbicide stays active in soil: low residual activity if rain or soil reactions neutralize it within weeks or months, high if it stays potent for the long term.

soil-applied herbicides.text: Herbicides applied to the soil before planting or crop emergence, taken up by the roots or shoots of emerging seedlings.

phosphorus leaching.text: The loss of phosphorus from fields by downward movement through the soil, an important pathway on flat, sandy land or soils prone to preferential flow.

salt tolerance of crops.text: The highest salt level a crop can withstand without losing productivity, beyond which it is harmed.

coir.text: Coconut husk fibre, whose processed form, coco peat, is used in potting mixes and as a substitute for peat.

land restoration.text: Returning land to a different or earlier state for an intended purpose, which may include renaturalisation or rewilding.

monoculture.text: Growing a single crop species in a field at one time.

dryland farming.text: Growing crops without irrigation, typically in regions where a cool wet season charges the soil with the moisture crops will use in the following dry season.

within-field variability.text: Differences in growing conditions within and between fields, which precision agriculture measures and manages.

saturated media extract.text: The main test of a potting mix's chemistry, which analyses a water extract of the mix.

specialty potting mixes.text: Growing media adapted to a plant's, or a growth stage's, needs for aeration, drainage, nutrition and pH.

agrominerals.text: Minerals, sometimes called stone bread, that matter to farming and horticulture because they can supply essential plant nutrients.

agrogeology.text: The study of agrominerals, the minerals that matter to farming, their origins and uses; more broadly, geology applied to farm soil productivity and health.

organic farming and soil quality.text: The dispute over whether organically managed soils end up better or worse than conventionally farmed ones.

organic soil fertility management.text: In organic farming, replacing the nutrients crops remove through the natural breakdown of organic matter, using green manure and composting.

center-pivot irrigation.text: Sprinkler irrigation from equipment that rotates around a central pivot, watering a circular area of crop.

soil remineralization.text: Replenishing a soil's mineral nutrients by working crushed rock powder into it.

basin irrigation.text: Surface irrigation in which a level area enclosed by earth banks is flooded quickly and the water left to soak in.

furrow irrigation.text: Surface irrigation through small parallel channels running down the field's main slope, with water flowing by gravity from the top end.

spate irrigation.text: Irrigation that diverts seasonal floods from normally dry river beds onto fields or into storage basins.

fallow syndrome.text: Poor nutrient uptake by a crop after a fallow period because the soil lacks arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.

fertigation.text: The injection of fertilizers and other water-soluble products into an irrigation system.

holistic planned grazing.text: Grazing that keeps rotating livestock herds between fields to mimic how natural herds graze.

alley cropping.text: Growing strips of crops between rows of closely spaced trees or hedges.

biofumigation.text: Pest control in which a fumigant gas comes from fresh plant material chopped and buried in the soil to decompose.

rock phosphate fertilizer.text: Phosphorite, a phosphorus-bearing sedimentary rock used as a sustainable, low-cost source of phosphorus for crops.

zaï.text: A farming technique of digging pits in poorly permeable soil to catch water and concentrate compost.

biosolarization.text: An alternative to soil fumigation that adds organic amendments or compost before solarizing, so that microbial activity shortens the treatment.

rotations and soil organic matter.text: Crop type, yield, root mass, harvested portion and residue management together set soil organic matter under a rotation.

cover crop functions by species.text: Different cover crop plants are grown for different primary purposes.

natural farming.text: An ecological farming approach set out by Masanobu Fukuoka, also called the Fukuoka method or do-nothing farming.

deficit irrigation.text: An irrigation strategy that waters a crop during its drought-sensitive growth stages and limits water at other times.

soilless growing substrates.text: Inert or organic materials such as perlite or gravel that mechanically support plant roots in hydroponics, where plants grow without soil.

cover crop nitrogen supply.text: Cover crops can supply nitrogen to the next crop or lower available nitrogen at season end to cut losses.

mineral wool growing medium.text: Mineral wool is a fibrous material spun or drawn from molten rock or slag, used among other things as a hydroponic growth medium.

expanded clay aggregate.text: A lightweight, porous aggregate made by heating clay to about 1,200 °C in a rotary kiln, often called LECA.

soil steaming methods.text: The ways of applying steam to soil, grouped as substrate, surface and deep soil steaming, chosen by soil structure, crop and area to treat.

grass cover crops.text: Grass cover crops include annual cereals (rye, wheat, triticale, barley, oats), forage grasses such as ryegrass, and warm-season grasses such as sorghum-sudangrass.

legume cover crops.text: Leguminous plants are often very good cover crops, grouped as summer annuals, winter annuals, and biennial or perennial legumes.

multiple cropping.text: Growing two or more crops on the same land within one year instead of just one.

methyl bromide.text: An organobromine gas, CH3Br, long used as a fumigant and soil sterilant.

variable rate application.text: Applying a material such as fertilizer at a rate that changes with the location or qualities of each part of a field, instead of uniformly.

soil salinity classes for crops.text: Bernstein's grouping of soils by the electrical conductivity of a saturated soil-paste extract (ECe), matched to the crops each class can still grow well.

crop tolerance to seawater.text: The ability of a crop to withstand the high salinity of irrigation with seawater or a mix of fresh water and seawater.

historic rotations and the corn-soybean.term: Historic rotations and the corn-soybean rotation
historic rotations and the corn-soybean.text: Rotations should suit each farm's soil, climate, resources and economics, so only historic examples can guide.

crop diversification.text: Cropping systems can be diversified over time, across the farm landscape, or with perennials, trees and livestock.

rotation design principles.text: A set of guidelines for designing a new crop rotation.

active rooting period.text: The active rooting period is the percent of a rotation during which living roots are present.

rotation labor and economics.text: Diversified rotations spread labor and reduce exposure to price swings, but add equipment and management demands.

rotations and water quality.text: Diversified rotations offer benefits over very simple ones, including better water quality and lower nitrous oxide loss.

cover crop management cautions.text: Cover crops can cause serious problems if not managed carefully.

cover crop mixtures.text: Mixtures of cover crop species offer combined benefits, the most common being a grass with a legume.

cover crop planting timing.text: A cover crop can be planted for a whole growing season, after the cash crop harvest, or interseeded into a growing cash crop.

cover crop termination.text: Cover crops are killed or drastically weakened before or during soil preparation for the next cash crop.

cover crops and plant-parasitic nematode.text: Cover crop choice can limit nematode damage, because species differ in host status.

planting green.text: Planting green is seeding a cash crop directly into a still-living cover crop and terminating the cover soon after.

buckwheat cover crop.text: Buckwheat is a frost-sensitive summer annual cover crop that completes its life cycle quickly.

cover crops in perennial systems.text: In orchards and vineyards, groundcover or floor management with perennial cover crops can improve soil health and crop quality.

rotation and plant disease control.text: Carefully chosen rotations, especially alternating grains and broadleaf plants, help control plant diseases and nematodes.

faidherbia albida in agroforestry.text: Faidherbia albida is a tropical legume tree of seasonally dry climates used in silvopasture and alley cropping.

forest farming.text: Forest farming grows understory crops within an established natural or timber forest, without separate growing zones.

silvopasture.text: Silvopasture integrates trees and grazing livestock on the same land.

tillage.text: The preparation of soil for farming by mechanically agitating it, for example by digging, stirring or overturning it.

agroecology.text: An academic discipline that studies ecological processes as they apply to agricultural production systems.

transitional agroforestry systems.text: Transitional systems exploit shading and microclimate change as trees mature.

agroecosystem.text: An ecological system that people manage and shape in order to farm.

soil sickness.text: A decline in soil fertility and crop yield, often after long-term monoculture, marked by a shift in harmful and beneficial soil microbes.

plough.text: A farm tool for loosening or turning over soil before sowing seed or planting.

arable land.text: Land that can be ploughed and used to grow crops.

effects of tillage.text: The consequences of tilling for a soil: it loosens and aerates the topsoil for planting, but it also degrades structure, speeds erosion and compacts the soil.

primary and secondary tillage.text: The division of tillage into deeper, more thorough primary operations and shallower, often more selective secondary ones.

harrow.text: A farm implement for surface tillage, used after ploughing to break up and smooth the soil surface.

contour plowing.text: Ploughing or planting across a slope along its elevation contour lines, also called contour farming.

crop residue.text: The stalks, stubble, leaves and other plant material left in a field after harvest.

conservation tillage.text: A group of practices that reduce tillage and leave at least 30% of crop residue, or at least 1,000 lb/ac (1,100 kg/ha) of small grain residue, on the surface during the critical erosion period.

no-till farming.text: A way of growing crops or pasture without disturbing the soil by tillage, also called zero tillage or direct drilling.

forest site preparation.text: Any of the treatments applied to a forest site to ready it for seeding or planting.

intensive tillage.text: Tillage that leaves less than 15% crop residue cover, or less than 500 pounds per acre (560 kg/ha) of small grain residue, on the soil.

mounding.text: A forest site-preparation treatment that builds raised planting spots, which have improved seedling performance on cold, wet sites.

no-till and soil carbon.text: The dispute over whether no-till farming really increases the organic carbon stored in soil.

reduced tillage.text: Tillage that leaves 15 to 30% crop residue cover, or 500 to 1000 pounds per acre (560 to 1100 kg/ha) of small grain residue, during the critical erosion period.

slash burning for site preparation.text: Broadcast or prescribed burning of logging slash on cleared forest sites to prepare them for planting or seeding.

tillage and archaeology.text: The damage tilling does to buried ancient remains such as long barrows.

mouldboard plough.text: A plough whose curved mould board lifts the slice of soil cut by the share and turns it over into the previous furrow.

weed management in no-till.text: Controlling weeds without tillage, using herbicides, cover crops, mowing or crimping in place of cultivation.

three-field system.text: A crop rotation in which a field grows one set of crops in the first year, a different set in the second and lies fallow in the third.

conversion to arable land.text: Making land that cannot grow crops capable of cultivation.

stubble burning.text: Deliberately setting fire to the straw stubble left after harvesting grains such as rice and wheat.

keyline design.text: P. A. Yeomans' system of planning farm landscapes around the natural flow of water to make the best use of their water resources.

ard.text: The early animal-drawn scratch plough, which drags a share through the topsoil to cut a shallow furrow.

chisel plough.text: A plough for deep tillage that loosens and aerates soil while leaving crop residue on the surface.

heavy plough.text: A wheeled plough heavy enough to carry a large metal-faced mould board and so to work the heavy soils of northern Europe.

hoe cultivation.text: Turning soil with hand-held digging sticks and hoes, the way soil was worked when agriculture began.

mole plough.text: A deep plough with a torpedo-shaped tip that leaves a drainage channel underground, or breaks up deep impermeable layers, without digging trenches.

cultivator.text: A farm implement for secondary tillage, either a frame with teeth dragged through the soil or a machine with rotating disks or teeth such as a rotary tiller.

vertical tillage.text: A set of tillage principles that, like conservation agriculture, aims to improve soil health, raise infiltration and reduce erosion and compaction.

optimum water content for tillage.text: The soil moisture content at which tillage breaks the soil into the largest number of small aggregates.

disc harrow.text: A harrow whose cutting edges are rows of concave metal discs set at an angle, used to till soil and chop weeds or crop residue.

seedbed.text: The local soil environment into which seeds are planted.

deep ploughing.text: Ploughing deeper than 50 cm, compared with ordinary ploughing that rarely goes below 20 cm.

minimum tillage.text: A soil conservation system that keeps soil manipulation to the minimum a crop needs, without turning the soil over.

strip-till.text: A minimum-tillage conservation system that tills only the narrow strip of soil that will hold the seed row, leaving the soil between rows untilled.

stubble mulching.text: Leaving stubble or crop residue in place on the land as a surface cover during a fallow period.

controlled traffic farming.text: A management system that confines all machinery loads to the smallest possible area of permanent traffic lanes, to limit soil damage from heavy or repeated passes.

mulch tillage.text: A seeding method in which the whole soil surface is tilled and crop residue mixed in, while some residue stays on the surface.

residue cover after tillage passes.text: Estimating the share of the soil surface still covered by crop residue after a sequence of tillage operations by multiplying each tool's remaining fraction.

subsoiling.text: Deep tillage with a subsoiler, an implement whose heavy shanks loosen and break up soil below the depth reached by ploughs, harrows or rototillers.

history of tillage.text: How tillage began with small-grain farmers and spread, from the ard and animal traction to the moldboard plough and powerful tractors.

frost tillage.text: Tilling soil after frost has entered it but before it has penetrated more than about 2 inches (5 cm).

plough pan.text: A compacted layer of soil created by tillage, also called a tillage pan.

ridge tillage.text: A conservation tillage system that builds ridges or beds for the seed zone and keeps fixed traffic lanes.

soil conservation.text: Preventing the loss of topsoil to erosion, and the loss of fertility through overuse, acidification, salinization or chemical contamination.

cover crop.text: A crop planted to cover the soil rather than to be harvested.

terrace (earthworks).text: A flat surface cut into a hill or mountainside for growing crops, usually built as a series of steps like a staircase.

soil management.text: Applying operations, practices and treatments to protect soil and improve its performance, such as its fertility or mechanical behaviour.

windbreak.text: One or more rows of trees or shrubs, also called a shelterbelt, planted to shelter land from the wind and protect soil from erosion.

agroforestry.text: A land use system that integrates trees with crops or pasture.

strip farming.text: Farming a field divided into long, narrow strips that alternate in a crop rotation, also called strip cropping.

soil stabilization.text: Any physical, chemical, mechanical or biological method, alone or combined, of altering a natural soil to meet an engineering purpose.

cover crops for soil fertility.text: Growing cover crops, often legumes, to raise soil fertility, chiefly by supplying or conserving nitrogen.

conservation agriculture.text: A farming system, as defined by the FAO, that prevents loss of arable land and regenerates degraded land through minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and diverse plant species.

reducing pesticide use.text: Cutting pesticide use to protect soil, since pesticides can contaminate soil, nearby vegetation and water for a long time.

soil-conservation farming.text: Farming that combines no-till, green manures and other soil-enhancing practices to protect and rebuild the soil.

soil management and greenhouse gases.text: The effect of how soils are managed on greenhouse gases: management can emit nitrous oxide and carbon, or store carbon dioxide as soil organic carbon.

lynchet.text: An earth terrace on a hillside, typical of the ancient field systems of the British Isles.

cover crops and soil water.text: The ways cover crops change how water enters, moves through and leaves a field's soil.

cover crops in pest and disease control.term: Cover crops in pest and disease control
cover crops in pest and disease control.text: Using cover crops to break pest and disease cycles, lure pests away as trap crops and attract their natural enemies.

buffer strip.text: A strip of land kept under permanent vegetation, mostly on farmland, to protect soil, water and air quality.

weed suppression by cover crops.text: The control of weeds by cover crops, through competition while they grow and smothering or chemical inhibition after they die.

biological pest control.text: A method of controlling animal pests, weeds or plant and animal pathogens by using other organisms.

contour trenching.text: Digging continuous trenches along the contour of a slope to conserve water and soil and raise crop yields, an easily applied technique in arid sub-Saharan areas.

soil conservation and domestic allotment.term: Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Act of 1936
soil conservation and domestic allotment.text: A US federal law of 1936 that let the government pay farmers to cut production in order to conserve soil and prevent erosion.

terracette.text: A landform of roughly parallel, step-like ridges on a steep hillside.

great plains shelterbelt.text: A US project, begun in 1934, to plant windbreaks across the Great Plains states.

check dam.text: A small, sometimes temporary dam built across a swale, ditch or waterway to counter erosion by slowing the water.

catch crop.text: A fast-growing crop, a type of cover crop, grown between two successive main crops.

structural and agronomic erosion control.text: Runoff and erosion control methods fall into structural measures, which are engineered works, and agronomic practices, which change soil and crop management.

off-site effects of soil erosion.text: Soil carried off fields harms places beyond the farm, as sediment fills streams, rivers, reservoirs and estuaries or blowing dust reaches towns.

magnesium chloride dust control.text: Spreading magnesium chloride on unpaved roads and dusty sites, where its moisture-absorbing nature keeps fine particles from becoming airborne.

mechanical soil stabilization.text: Strengthening a soil layer by confining the movement of its particles, for example with geogrids or three-dimensional geocells.

prairie strips.text: Strips of native perennial vegetation placed within row-crop fields to protect soil and water and support biodiversity.

bioretention.text: Removing sediment and contaminants from stormwater runoff by passing it through planted soil, where plants and microbes hold and break down pollutants.

contour buffer strip.text: Strips of perennial vegetation alternating with wider cultivated strips of cropland across a slope.

filter strip.text: A band of grass or other permanent vegetation at a field's edge that shields riparian areas from sediment, pesticides, pathogens and nutrients in runoff.

accelerated erosion on farmland.text: Erosion is a natural geological process, but farming greatly accelerates it, especially where soil is bare.

extreme events and erosion.text: Most erosion damage comes from rare extreme weather events, so its risk is easy to underestimate.

vetiver system.text: A soil and water conservation system built on hedgerows of the vetiver grass.

soil survey.text: The process of classifying the soil types and other soil properties of an area and recording them geographically; also called soil mapping.

soil map.text: A geographical representation of the soil types, or of soil properties such as pH, texture, organic matter or horizon depth, across an area.

prime farmland.text: A US Department of Agriculture designation for land with the best combination of physical and chemical characteristics for producing food, feed, forage, fibre and oilseed crops, and available for those uses.

land use.text: A description of what people do on a parcel of land, covering the benefits taken from it and the management actions applied.

remote sensing.text: Gathering information about an object or area from a distance, usually with sensors on satellites or aircraft, instead of measuring it on site.

geographic information system.text: Integrated computer hardware and software that store, manage, analyse, edit and display geographic data.

digital soil mapping.text: The computer-assisted production of digital maps of soil types and soil properties, also called predictive soil mapping.

soil value.text: Germany's comparative rating of soil quality (Bodenwertzahl), scored from soil sampling data on a scale from 0 (very low) to 100 (very high).

soil survey interpretation.text: The use of soil survey information to predict the potentials and limitations of soils for particular uses, such as crops, building or gardens.

digital elevation model.text: A computer representation of elevation data that depicts terrain, or the objects on top of it.

european soil database.text: The only harmonized soil database in Europe, the source of many other soil data, information and services.

ssurgo.text: The Soil Survey Geographic database, digital soil data produced and distributed in the United States by the Natural Resources Conservation Service.

pedometrics.text: The application of mathematical and statistical methods to the study of the distribution and genesis of soils.

pedometric mapping.text: Data-driven production of soil property and soil class maps by statistical methods, also called statistical soil mapping.

universal model of soil variation.text: A model that splits a soil variable at any place into a deterministic trend, a spatially autocorrelated random part and leftover noise: Z(s) = m(s) + ε′(s) + ε″.

land use change.text: The change from one land-use category to another, mostly driven by human activity.

aerial photography.text: Taking photographs of landscapes and surface features from aircraft or other airborne platforms.

land suitability classification.text: An FAO method of land evaluation that appraises and groups areas of land by their fitness for a defined use.

site index.text: A forestry measure of a site's potential for tree growth, given as the height of dominant and co-dominant trees at a base age.

storie index.text: A soil rating method based on the soil characteristics that govern a land's potential use and productive capacity.

land use capability map.text: A map showing the potential uses, usually for farming, of each unit of land.

soil phase.text: A subdivision of a soil series made when slope, erosion, stoniness or another feature changes how the soil can be used.

reconnaissance soil survey.text: A small-scale soil survey of low-value land that identifies regions dominated by soil associations rather than delineating individual soils.

web soil survey.text: An online service run by the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service that gives access to soil data from the National Cooperative Soil Survey.

fao land suitability classes.text: The numbered degrees of suitability within each FAO land suitability order, in decreasing order of suitability.

soil information system.text: A systematic, consistent collection of gridded or vector soil property and class maps, with attached report, manual or metadata, covering a whole area of interest.

site index curves and equations.text: Graphs or equations that convert a stand's measured dominant height and age into its site index.

inductively coupled plasma atomic emissi.term: Inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy
inductively coupled plasma atomic emissi.text: An analytical technique (ICP-AES or ICP-OES) that detects chemical elements from the light emitted by atoms and ions excited in an argon plasma.

gas chromatography.text: Chromatography that separates and analyses compounds that can be vaporized without decomposing.

elemental analysis.text: Analysis of a material such as soil for its elemental, and sometimes isotopic, composition.

inductively coupled plasma mass spectrom.text: Mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) that ionizes a sample in an inductively coupled plasma and counts the resulting ions to detect metals and some non-metals at very low concentrations.

loss on ignition.text: A test that strongly heats a soil or mineral sample at a set temperature until its mass stops changing, so the weight lost measures the volatile components driven off.

kjeldahl method.text: A wet-chemistry method that measures the organic nitrogen plus ammonia and ammonium in a sample.

soil test calibration.text: The multi-year matching of a soil test value to crop yield response, which is what makes the test value meaningful.

soil sampling for fertility testing.text: Collecting a representative composite of soil cores from a field so a laboratory can evaluate fertility.

atomic absorption spectroscopy.text: An elemental analysis method that measures the concentration of metals in a sample from the light their atoms absorb.

soil test phosphorus methods.text: Regional chemical extractions used to estimate plant-available phosphorus, with different numeric ranges for each extractant.

ion chromatography.text: Chromatography that separates ions and ionizable molecules by their affinity for an ion exchanger.

sample preparation.text: The treatment a sample receives before analysis so that it is in a form the instrument can measure.

certified reference materials.text: Controls or standards of known composition used to check the quality and traceability of measurements, validate methods and calibrate instruments.

soil test interpretation categories.text: Labs sort each test value into categories from very low to excessive, each tied to the probability that adding the nutrient will raise yield.

unusual soil test results.text: Odd soil test values that usually trace to management history or to using the wrong extractant for the soil.

crop nitrogen sensing.text: In-season technologies that assess a crop's nitrogen status to guide fertilizer rates.

grid soil sampling.text: Sampling a large field on a grid and analysing each point separately to guide site-specific nutrient and lime rates.

high tunnel soil testing.text: High tunnel soils need adjusted tests because very high yields demand much more nutrient and rain does not leach salts.

fine earth fraction.text: The part of a soil made of particles 2 mm across or smaller.

soil thin section.text: A slice of rock, mineral or soil ground to about 30 μm and mounted on glass for study under a polarizing microscope.

ion-selective electrode.text: A membrane-based potentiometric sensor that converts the activity of a specific ion in solution into an electrical potential.

ammonium acetate extraction.text: The use of ammonium acetate solution in soil analysis to displace exchangeable cations, for measuring CEC and available potassium.

molybdenum blue phosphate test.text: A colorimetric test in which phosphate forms a blue molybdenum complex whose depth of colour is proportional to phosphorus concentration.

soil micromorphology.text: The description, measurement and interpretation of soil features too small to see with the unaided eye.

digital image analysis.text: Image analysis extracts meaningful information from images, mainly digital ones, by digital image processing.

soil biofabric.text: Soil fabric made by organisms, typically small, often pelleted micro- and mesobiofabric left by ants, worms and termites and seen with a hand lens or in soil thin sections.

polarized light microscopy.text: Polarized light microscopy covers optical microscopy techniques that illuminate a sample with polarized light, most useful on birefringent samples.

mineral alteration in thin section.text: The changes natural processes make to a mineral's chemical composition or crystal structure, as they appear under the microscope.

x-ray microtomography.text: X-ray microtomography uses X-rays to make cross-sections of an object at micrometre pixel size and rebuild a 3D model without destroying the sample.

spatial analysis.text: Spatial analysis is any of the formal techniques that study entities using their topological, geometric or geographic properties.

geomorphometry.text: The science of measuring the shape of the land surface and the effects of that shape on human and natural processes.

landsat program.text: The Landsat program is the longest-running enterprise that has acquired satellite imagery of Earth.

ground-penetrating radar.text: A geophysical method that images the subsurface with radar pulses, recording reflections from buried boundaries.

scorpan model.text: The scorpan model, proposed by McBratney and colleagues in 2003, extends Jenny's clorpt model so that soil-environment relationships can be applied digitally.

conventional soil mapping.text: Conventional soil mapping is the surveyor-led production of soil maps from field inspections, building on Jenny's soil-forming factors and national taxonomic systems.

electromagnetic induction.text: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force across a conductor in a changing magnetic field.

electrical resistivity tomography.text: A geophysical technique that images subsurface structure from electrical resistivity measured with electrodes at the surface or in boreholes.

digital soil map accuracy assessment.text: Accuracy assessment measures how far a digital soil map's predicted values differ from observed ones, using an independent validation dataset.

digital soil map uncertainty.text: Digital soil map uncertainty is the error that accumulates in a predicted soil map, which should be estimated as carefully as it is validated.

spatial scale.text: Spatial scale describes or categorises the size of a space, or the extent at which a phenomenon or process occurs.

multispectral imaging.text: Imaging that captures data in a small number of separate wavelength bands, typically 3 to 15, including bands beyond visible light.

spatial variability.text: The way a quantity measured at different places takes different values from place to place.

hyperspectral imaging.text: Imaging that records a full, finely resolved spectrum across many continuous bands for each pixel, to identify materials or detect processes.

normalized difference vegetation index.text: A widely used remote-sensing measure of the health and density of vegetation, calculated from the red and near-infrared bands.

modifiable areal unit problem.text: The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) is a source of statistical bias that arises when point-based measures are aggregated into areal units.

geostatistics.text: A branch of statistics that deals with spatial or spatio-temporal data sets.

variogram.text: A graph or function describing how much pairs of observations differ according to the distance separating them, the key tool of geostatistics.

kriging.text: A geostatistical interpolation method that predicts a value at an unsampled point as a weighted average of nearby known values, based on a model of their covariance.

spatial interpolation.text: Estimating the values of a quantity at arbitrary places from values known at a set of points, when the variables are spatial coordinates.

regression-kriging.text: A spatial prediction technique that regresses the target variable on auxiliary variables, such as terrain and remote-sensing layers, and then kriges the regression residuals.

random forest.text: Random forest is an ensemble learning method for classification and regression that builds many decision trees during training.

inverse distance weighting.text: A deterministic interpolation method that estimates unknown values as a weighted average of known points, each weighted by the inverse of its distance.

spatial autocorrelation.text: Spatial dependency is the co-variation of properties across geographic space, so characteristics at nearby locations appear correlated, positively or negatively.

stratified sampling.text: Stratified sampling samples a population that can be partitioned into subpopulations by sampling each stratum independently.

compositional data.text: Compositional data are quantitative descriptions of the parts of some whole, conveying relative information.

log-ratio transformation.text: Log-ratio transformations map compositions from the simplex into real space so ordinary statistics can be applied.

soil survey intensity levels.text: Survey intensity levels grade how densely a conventional soil survey is checked in the field.

sampling design.text: A sampling design specifies for every possible sample its probability of being drawn.

soil sampling design for digital soil ma.term: Soil sampling design for digital soil mapping
soil sampling design for digital soil ma.text: Sampling design for digital soil mapping selects sites representative of the geographic area and of the soil-forming factors (covariates) being modelled.

topographic wetness index.text: A steady-state wetness index, computed from slope and upslope contributing area, that quantifies topographic control on hydrological processes.

fuzzy clustering.text: Fuzzy clustering, also called soft clustering, is a form of clustering in which each data point can belong to more than one cluster.

soilgrids.text: A system for automated global soil mapping based on models fitted to soil profiles and environmental covariate data.

planetary gamma-ray spectrometry.text: The use of orbiting gamma-ray spectrometers to map the elements of planetary surfaces, especially the Moon and Mars.

latin hypercube sampling.text: Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) is a statistical method for generating a near-random sample of parameter values from a multidimensional distribution.

uncertainty quantification.text: Uncertainty quantification is the science of quantitatively characterising and estimating uncertainties in computational and real-world applications.

near-infrared spectroscopy.text: A spectroscopic method using the near-infrared part of the spectrum, from 780 nm to 2500 nm.

carbon cycle.text: The part of Earth's biogeochemical cycles in which carbon moves among living things, soils, rocks, water and the atmosphere.

chemometrics.text: Chemometrics is the science of extracting information from chemical systems by data-driven means.

partial least squares regression.text: Partial least squares (PLS) regression is a reduced-rank method that projects both predictors and responses into new spaces to find the relation between them.

multivariate calibration.text: Multivariate calibration builds models that predict a property of interest from measured responses such as spectra.

soil carbon.text: The solid carbon stored in soils, both as organic matter from plants, animals and microbes and as inorganic carbonate minerals.

carbon sink.text: A natural or artificial process that removes a greenhouse gas, or a substance that forms one, from the atmosphere, taking up more carbon than it releases.

carbon sequestration.text: The storing of carbon in a carbon pool, which limits climate change by reducing carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

climate change mitigation.text: Action to limit the greenhouse gases in the atmosphere that cause climate change, also called decarbonisation.

soil carbon and climate change.text: The two-way link between climate and soil carbon: climate change alters soils and their carbon, and soil carbon losses or gains alter the climate.

effects of climate change on agriculture.term: Effects of climate change on agriculture
effects of climate change on agriculture.text: The many ways a changing climate alters farming, most of them making it harder for agriculture to provide global food security.

soil inorganic carbon.text: Carbon held in soil as minerals, mainly carbonates, formed by weathering of parent material or by soil minerals reacting with atmospheric CO2.

soil organic carbon.text: The carbon held in soil organic matter, which is about 50% carbon by dry weight.

managing soil carbon.text: Choosing land and farm practices to avoid losses of soil organic carbon and to build it up.

permafrost carbon cycle.text: The Arctic part of the global carbon cycle, in which carbon moves from permafrost soils to plants, microbes and the air and back into frozen soil by burial.

active layer.text: The top layer of soil in permafrost regions that thaws each summer and freezes again in autumn.

soils as carbon sinks.text: The role of soils as a short- to long-term carbon store holding more carbon than all land vegetation and the atmosphere combined.

pingo.text: An ice-cored hill, 3–70 m high and 30–1,000 m across, that grows only in permafrost.

soil carbon sequestration.text: Drawing carbon dioxide from the air into soil, where plants fix it as organic carbon; it is a major soil property and an ecosystem service.

soil carbon feedback.text: The release of carbon from soils in response to global warming, which in turn adds to warming.

permafrost thaw.text: The warming and thawing of permafrost under climate change, seen as a thickening active layer and shrinking frozen ground.

permafrost zones.text: The division of permafrost regions by how much of the land is underlain by permafrost: continuous, discontinuous, sporadic and isolated.

fast and slow carbon cycles.text: The split of the carbon cycle into a fast biological cycle that turns over in years and a slow geological cycle that takes millions of years.

carbon catchment health.text: The wider benefits to soil and catchment health that come from raising soil carbon, beyond its role as a carbon sink.

soil carbon monitoring.text: Estimating soil organic carbon stocks and their changes by field survey and modelling, as climate reporting requires.

soil organic carbon and soil function.term: Soil organic carbon and soil function
soil organic carbon and soil function.text: The way organic carbon sustains a soil's ability to provide services, a capacity known as soil health.

climate change feedbacks.text: Natural processes that change how much the planet warms for a given amount of greenhouse gas emissions; positive feedbacks amplify warming and negative ones damp it.

methane emissions.text: The release of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, to the atmosphere from human activities and natural sources such as wetlands.

terrestrial carbon pool.text: The carbon held on land, in all living and dead land organisms and in soils.

carbon pool.text: Any reservoir in the Earth system where carbon resides in some chemical form for a period of time.

land-use change and carbon loss.text: The release of land carbon to the atmosphere when people clear or convert vegetation, chiefly by turning forest into farmland or towns.

alpine permafrost.text: Permafrost found at high elevations, in mountains cold enough to keep the ground frozen year after year.

construction on permafrost.text: Engineering methods for building on permafrost without thawing the frozen ground that supports the structure.

history of permafrost research.text: The development of permafrost science from early Siberian reports to modern international collaboration.

massive ground ice.text: Permafrost so rich in ice that ice exceeds 250 percent of the dry soil by mass.

yedoma.text: Ice-rich, organic-rich permafrost of Pleistocene age, about 2% carbon by mass with 50–90% ice by volume.

past extent of permafrost.text: The much larger area that permafrost covered during the Last Glacial Maximum.

permafrost base depth.text: The depth at which Earth's geothermal heat balances the mean surface temperature at 0 °C, marking the bottom of permafrost.

permafrost ecology.text: How permanently frozen ground shapes the plants, animals and microbes that live with it.

permafrost landforms.text: The surface features built by freezing, cracking and thawing of permafrost ground.

permafrost thaw and infrastructure.text: The threat that thawing permafrost poses to settlements, roads, pipelines and buildings built on frozen ground.

pollutants released by permafrost thaw.text: Toxic waste and natural mercury held in frozen ground that thaw could release into the environment.

revival of ancient organisms from permaf.term: Revival of ancient organisms from permafrost
revival of ancient organisms from permaf.text: The survival of ancient microbes and plant tissue in frozen ground, and their possible revival when permafrost thaws.

subsea permafrost.text: Permafrost beneath the seabed of polar continental shelves, on land exposed during the Last Glacial Maximum and since flooded.

methanotroph.text: Bacteria or archaea that use methane as their source of carbon and energy.

mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storag.term: Mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storage
mycorrhizal fungi and soil carbon storag.text: The part that root-associated mycorrhizal fungi play in building, keeping and losing the soil carbon pool.

agricultural greenhouse gas emissions.text: The greenhouse gases released by farming, including from agricultural soils and from clearing land for crops.

thaw-induced ground instability.text: The weakening and movement of ground as its permafrost ice thaws and drains.

wetland restoration.text: Restoring wetlands and peatlands so that they keep sequestering carbon and storing water.

climate tipping points.text: A critical threshold that, when crossed, leads to large, accelerating and often irreversible changes in the climate system.

permafrost carbon release.text: The escape of long-stored carbon from thawing permafrost soils to the atmosphere as microbes decompose it.

climate change and soil fertility.text: The decline in soil quality expected as warming brings heavier rain and faster decay of soil organic matter.

sea level rise and farmland.text: The loss of low-lying farmland to flooding, erosion and salt as sea levels rise.

thawing of potentially arable land.text: The prospect that climate change will open new farmland as frozen ground in the far north thaws.

permafrost carbon feedback.text: The warming caused when thawing permafrost releases its stored carbon as carbon dioxide and methane, which in turn drives more thaw.

permafrost carbon stocks.text: The amount of organic carbon held in permafrost-region soils and deposits, more than twice the carbon in the atmosphere.

thermokarst.text: Irregular terrain of marshy hollows and small hummocks formed when ice-rich permafrost thaws.

talik.text: A zone of ground that stays unfrozen all year within a permafrost area.

soil carbon sponge.text: Porous, well-aggregated, healthy soil that absorbs and holds water well.

thaw depth.text: The level down to which soil has warmed to zero degrees Celsius at a given moment, separating thawed soil from frozen soil below.

syngenetic permafrost growth.text: Growth of permafrost upward as new material is deposited on a site under freezing conditions.

permafrost carbon dioxide emissions.text: The carbon dioxide released by aerobic microbial respiration in thawed permafrost soils, the bulk of permafrost emissions.

permafrost carbon storage processes.text: The two processes, syngenetic permafrost growth and cryoturbation, that carry plant-derived carbon down into permafrost for storage.

permafrost methane emissions.text: The methane produced by anaerobic microbes in waterlogged thawed permafrost, especially under thermokarst lakes.

arctic methane emissions.text: Methane released in the Arctic, mainly from thawing permafrost, melting sea ice, clathrate breakdown and the melting Greenland ice sheet, which adds to atmospheric methane.

land use, land-use change, and forestry.term: Land use, land-use change, and forestry
land use, land-use change, and forestry.text: The greenhouse gas inventory sector covering emissions and removals that result from human land use, land-use change and forestry.

abrupt permafrost thaw.text: Rapid thaw by hillside collapse (retrogressive thaw slumps) and thermokarst lake formation, which can expose deep soil to microbes within days.

permafrost emission estimates.text: Projections of the total greenhouse gases that thawing permafrost will release over this century and beyond.

black carbon in soils.text: Fire-derived carbon, from vegetation fires or deposited from the air, held in soil as charcoal particles and soot.

pereletok.text: A layer of frozen ground that stays frozen through several summers but eventually thaws.

soil formation in the active layer.term: Soil formation in the active layer
soil formation in the active layer.text: The cold-climate soil-forming processes, dominated by frost churning, that act in the seasonally thawed layer above permafrost.

compost-bomb instability.text: A proposed tipping point at which warming triggers runaway, explosive releases of soil carbon from peatlands.

carbon cycle feedbacks.text: The positive and negative climate feedbacks that come from Earth's carbon cycle, mostly negative so far.

biochar permanence.text: How long the carbon locked in biochar stays stored before returning to the atmosphere, the key measure of its durability as carbon removal.

enhanced weathering.text: A carbon dioxide removal method that speeds up natural weathering by spreading finely ground silicate rock, such as basalt, so that it reacts with water and air.

biochar carbon credits.text: Certified credits sold for carbon dioxide removed by producing biochar and storing it durably, traded on voluntary carbon markets.

silicate weathering and carbon dioxide.text: The natural removal of atmospheric CO2 when carbonic acid in rain and groundwater dissolves silicate and carbonate minerals.

mineral carbonation.text: The deliberate dissolution and carbonation of silicate minerals to lock CO2 into carbonate.

terrestrial enhanced weathering.text: Enhanced weathering done on land by spreading crushed silicate minerals over the ground surface.

supra-permafrost talik.text: An unfrozen layer that forms between the seasonally frozen surface and the permafrost when summer-thawed ground fails to refreeze in winter.

mycorrhizal fungi and soil aggregation.text: The way mycorrhizal fungi help bind soil into aggregates that physically shield organic carbon from microbial decay.
